security_spec.violation_condition: IOPMP hardware checker RTL implemented against the pre-PR spec where instruction fetch permission checking is gated behind HWCFG2[26] (chk_x). Post-PR, chk_x is removed and bit 26 becomes reserved. If the RTL still evaluates chk_x as an internal enable signal for the x-permission check datapath — and software compliant with the new spec leaves HWCFG2[26]=0 (as reserved bits should be zero) — the entire instruction fetch permission checking pipeline is silently disabled. Every instruction fetch transaction passes regardless of ENTRY_CFG.x or no_x settings, because the hardware AND-gate at the check output is driven by chk_x=0.
security_spec.summary: Removal of chk_x gating bit from baseline creates silent instruction-fetch bypass if RTL still uses HWCFG2[26] as fetch-check enable; software writes 0 to reserved bits but hardware interprets it as 'disable all instruction fetch checking'

findings.finding: chk_x hardwired to 0 ('unsupport instruction fetch check'). Post-PR per v0.8.2, instruction fetch permission (ENTRY_CFG.x, ttype=0x03, etype=0x03) is baseline. Hardwiring chk_x=0 means every instruction fetch silently bypasses all x-permission checking.
findings.snippet:
val chk_x = 0    // [R   ] unsupport instruction fetch check
val no_x  = 0    // [R   ] unsupport instruction fetch check

spec_citations.excerpt: ENTRY_CFG: struct { uint32_t x : 1; /* The instruction fetch permission to the protected memory region. */ ...}

findings.finding: chk_x and no_x are bit-packed into HWCFG0 (offset 0x0008, bits 10-11) instead of HWCFG3 (offset 0x0010, bits 27-28 per v0.8.2). The CSR offset is wrong and fields are in the wrong register. Software reading the spec-defined CSR address will see unrelated bits.
findings.snippet: def toUInt: UInt = Cat(..., no_w, no_x, chk_x, rrid_transl_prog, ...)

spec_citations.excerpt: HWCFG3: xinr at bit 27, no_x at bit 28, no_w at bit 29. chk_x is removed post-PR; instruction fetch is baseline.

findings.finding: The FSM permission check only evaluates entry_attribute.r (read) and entry_attribute.w (write). entry_attribute.x is read from SRAM (line 429) and latched (line 1272) but never evaluated. No etype=0x3 (illegal instruction fetch) is ever assigned. Every instruction fetch passes unchecked.

spec_citations.excerpt: etype: 0x03 = illegal instruction fetch. RTL never sets etype to 0x3.

findings.finding: ReqBundle has only 'rw' (Bool) to distinguish read vs write. No field encodes instruction-fetch transaction type. The bridge cannot communicate the transaction type needed for x-permission checking to the checker.

spec_citations.excerpt: Enumerates transaction types: read, write, instruction fetch (INSTR_FETCH = 3).

findings.finding: RspBundle has only cf_r and cf_w (check-fail flags). cf_x (check-fail for instruction fetch) is missing. Even if the checker detected a fetch violation, there is no response channel to carry it to the bridge.

spec_citations.excerpt: etype 0x03 = illegal instruction fetch. Requires cf_x in response bundle.

findings.finding: ttype is derived from req.rw: write→0x2, else→0x1 (read). No path to set ttype=0x3 (instruction fetch). Instruction fetch violations would be mis-logged as read violations in ERR_INFO.ttype.

spec_citations.excerpt: ttype: 0x03 = instruction fetch. RTL only encodes 0x01 and 0x02.

findings.finding: Interrupt decision checks sire (suppress read irq) and siwe (suppress write irq) but never sixe (suppress instruction fetch irq). entry_attribute.sixe is read from SRAM (line 433) but dead — never evaluated.

spec_citations.excerpt: sixe: Suppress interrupt on an illegal instruction fetch caught by the entry. RTL never checks this bit.
